articles.title: Waste Reduction in the Kitchen
articles.summary: This article provides practical strategies for restaurant operators to minimize food waste and maximize profits through better production control, creative use of leftovers, organized storage systems, and forward-thinking menu planning. It emphasizes how effective waste management can help restaurants improve their typically slim 4-5% profit margins.
keyPoints: Control waste during production through proper portioning, tracking prep waste, and monitoring cooking standards
Be creative with trim and leftovers by turning them into soups, stocks, daily specials, and blended beverages
Get organized with well-structured storage, inventory management, and rotation systems to prevent spoilage
Think ahead by planning ingredient flow through multiple menu applications and using equipment like Vitamix machines for repurposing
articles.mainContent: The restaurant business is notoriously tough, with retained profits typically running at just 4 to 5 percent of gross revenues, according to Forbes. To put it another way, plan on $100,000 of revenue for every $5,000 of year-end profit. That's a difficult line to walk and anything you can do to address waste reduction in the kitchen will help keep you in business. Controlling Waste During Production: Your food-cost calculations were based on getting a set yield from every ingredient you buy. Unless you track waste continuously, you won't know how accurate these numbers are. Haste leads to sloppy peeling and cutting, and this can drive up your cost on produce, meats and everything else you prepare in-house. Assign each cook a prep bucket for trim and wastage. Review it regularly to make sure they're meeting your standards. Poor portion-size management can also be an issue. Use a scale to check your cooks' portioning of costly meats and fish. Use standardized serving utensils that also act as portioning tools for your side dishes.

articles.title: What is the Slow Food Movement?
articles.summary: The Slow Food Movement, founded in 1986 by Carlo Petrini, promotes whole foods, clean production methods, and fair pricing in opposition to fast food culture. Restaurants can embrace Slow Food principles by using locally sourced ingredients, respecting environmental conservation, and making whole foods accessible to guests at reasonable prices.
keyPoints: Founded in 1986 in response to McDonald's proposed location at Spanish Steps in Rome, now operates in over 160 countries
Based on three fundamental tenets: whole foods, clean production methods that preserve environment, and fair pricing for consumers and producers
Restaurants can implement Slow Food by sourcing locally, educating staff, and incorporating principles into menu without unnecessary price increases
articles.mainContent: Foodies are a fickle lot. Nouvelle cuisine, gourmet comfort foods and deep fried candy bars — once the trending darlings of the culinary scene — are now all but extinct. The Slow Food movement, however, has surpassed the fad phase and laid down roots in the culinary world. In 1986, Carlo Petrini conceived the Slow Food Movement in defiance of a proposed McDonald's at the base of the Spanish Steps in Rome. Three years later, the movement formally established itself with the signing of the Slow Food Manifesto in Paris. Though modest in its beginnings, Slow Food now has national associations in over 160 countries. In 2013, the United Nations Environment Programme bestowed Petrini with its highest honor, the Champions of the Earth award, for his work in the movement. The Slow Food movement is much more than a farm-to-table approach to cuisine. The movement bases itself on three fundamental tenets: whole foods in the food service industry and at home, clean production methods that preserve the environment and fair pricing for both consumers and producers.

articles.title: How to Become a Certified Green Restaurant®
articles.summary: Chef Jonathon Sawyer opened The Greenhouse Tavern in Cleveland, Ohio as the first Certified Green Restaurant® in the state, featuring sustainable practices, farm-to-table ingredients, and a rooftop garden. The article explains the certification process which requires accumulating 100 GreenPoints™ across seven categories including water efficiency, waste reduction, and sustainable food practices.
keyPoints: The Greenhouse Tavern became Ohio's first Certified Green Restaurant® in 2009 with sustainable design and rooftop garden
Green certification requires 100 GreenPoints™ across seven categories: water efficiency, waste reduction, sustainable food, energy, and more
Restaurants must meet minimum requirements including full recycling programs, no polystyrene foam, and continuous improvement over 6 years
articles.mainContent: When Jonathon Sawyer and his wife, Amelia, returned to their hometown of Cleveland, Ohio to open a restaurant, they knew they wanted to design a concept around sustainable, farm-to-table living. That meant sourcing locally grown ingredients, environmentally conscious finishes, and durable kitchen equipment. The Greenhouse Tavern opened in 2009, honored as the first Certified Green Restaurant® in the state of Ohio, complete with a rooftop garden to provide the restaurant's herbs. There are three main levels of Certified Green Restaurants®: 2-, 3-, and 4-stars. Restaurants are awarded a certain number of points across seven categories, according to predetermined standards. The categories are: Water Efficiency, Waste Reduction & Recycling, Sustainable Durable Goods & Building Materials, Sustainable Food, Energy, Reusables & Environmentally Preferable Disposables, and Chemical & Pollution Reduction. To receive certification, a restaurant must: Accumulate a total of 100 GreenPoints™, Meet Minimum Green Points™ in each category (10 points in each), Have a full-scale recycling program, Be free of polystyrene foam (styrofoam), Yearly Education, Continual Change: By the end of Year 3, restaurant must have 135 GreenPoints™, By the end of Year 6, restaurant must have 175 GreenPoints™.

articles.title: Chef Chris Aquilino's Journey from Passion to Purpose
articles.summary: Chef Chris Aquilino, corporate executive chef at Envision Group/Compass Group, uses his artistic background and Vitamix equipment to create nutrient-dense meals for hospital patients while reducing food waste. He develops creative dishes using typically discarded produce parts like asparagus stems and broccoli stalks.
keyPoints: Chef Aquilino transitioned from fine arts to culinary arts, applying creative principles to food service
Uses Vitamix blenders to create smooth, nutrient-dense meals for hospital patients with modified texture diets
Implements zero-waste cooking practices using stems, stalks and food scraps to reduce 25% of food waste by 2020
articles.mainContent: At a young age, Chris Aquilino wanted to know how things worked, how to break them apart and rebuild them. This natural drive and curiosity spurred his desire to explore art, more specifically, sculpting. Through this medium, he learned the creative process and how to manipulate a raw ingredient into something he could truly identify with. As Aquilino grew up, he applied his creative talents to the kitchen, shifting his medium of choice to food, instead of clay. While it may be a disconnect to some, to Aquilino, the parallel between art and food is clear. "Whether it's clay, paint or food, the creative goal is usually the same — to make something beautiful that affects someone's mood, to really intersect with people in a more powerful and emotional way," he says. Now, as the corporate executive chef of Envision Group, a division of Compass Group, the world's largest foodservice corporation, Aquilino has the ability to do just that.
